logic_node.action_detail: In patients with HFrEF and iron deficiency (ferritin <100 mcg/L, or 100-300 mcg/L with transferrin saturation <20%), with or without anemia, intravenous iron replacement is reasonable to improve functional status and quality of life. Oral iron is not adequate.

source_text: In patients with HFrEF and iron deficiency with or without anemia, intravenous iron replacement is reasonable to improve functional status and QOL. Iron deficiency is usually defined as ferritin level <100 mcg/L or 100 to 300 mcg/L, if the transferrin saturation is <20%.

logic_node.action: Define iron deficiency criteria in HF
logic_node.action_detail: Iron deficiency in HF is defined as ferritin level <100 mcg/L, or ferritin 100-300 mcg/L if transferrin saturation is <20%. Routine baseline assessment of all patients with HF includes evaluation for anemia.

source_text: Iron deficiency is usually defined as ferritin level <100 mcg/L or 100 to 300 mcg/L, if the transferrin saturation is <20%. Routine baseline assessment of all patients with HF includes an evaluation for anemia.

logic_node.action: Do not use oral iron for iron deficiency in HF
logic_node.action_detail: Oral iron supplementation is not adequate to treat iron deficiency in patients with HF due to poor absorption and inadequacy to replete iron stores. The IRONOUT HF trial showed no improvement with oral iron.

source_text: The IRONOUT HF trial showed no such improvement with oral iron supplementation. This is attributed to the poor absorption of oral iron and inadequacy of oral iron to replete the iron stores in patients with HF.

logic_node.action: Do not use erythropoietin-stimulating agents in HF with anemia
logic_node.action_detail: In patients with HF and anemia, erythropoietin-stimulating agents (e.g., darbepoetin alfa) should not be used to improve morbidity and mortality. A randomized trial of 2278 patients showed no benefit and an increase in thrombotic events including stroke.

source_text: In patients with HF and anemia, erythropoietin-stimulating agents should not be used to improve morbidity and mortality. A high-quality randomized trial of darbepoetin alpha in 2278 patients showed no benefit and an increase in thrombotic events, including stroke.

logic_node.action: Uptitrate GDMT to maximally tolerated target dose for hypertension
logic_node.action_detail: In patients with HFrEF and hypertension, uptitration of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) to the maximally tolerated target dose is recommended, targeting goal blood pressures defined by ACC/AHA hypertension guidelines.

source_text: In patients with HFrEF and hypertension, uptitration of GDMT to the maximally tolerated target dose is recommended. Hypertension in patients with HFrEF represents an opportunity to maximize GDMT to goal blood pressures defined by the ACC/AHA hypertension guidelines.

logic_node.action_detail: In patients with HF and suspicion of sleep-disordered breathing, a formal sleep assessment is reasonable to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate between obstructive and central sleep apnea. Daytime sleepiness may not reflect the degree of underlying sleep-disordered breathing.

source_text: In patients with HF and suspicion of sleep-disordered breathing, a formal sleep assessment is reasonable to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate between obstructive and central sleep apnea.

logic_node.action: Consider CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea in HF
logic_node.action_detail: In patients with HF and obstructive sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) may be reasonable to improve sleep quality and decrease daytime sleepiness. Meta-analyses show moderate reduction in BNP and improvement in blood pressure and LVEF.

source_text: In patients with HF and obstructive sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure may be reasonable to improve sleep quality and decrease daytime sleepiness. Meta-analyses of RCTs have shown positive airway pressure therapy results in moderate reduction in BNP.

logic_node.action: Do not use adaptive servo-ventilation in HFrEF with central sleep apnea
logic_node.action_detail: In patients with NYHA class II-IV HFrEF and central sleep apnea, adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) causes harm and should not be used. ASV was associated with increased mortality in 2 RCTs (including SERVE-HF and CAT-HF trials).

source_text: In patients with NYHA class II to IV HFrEF and central sleep apnea, adaptive servo-ventilation causes harm. Adaptive servo-ventilation was associated with increased mortality in 2 RCTs involving patients with HFrEF and central sleep apnea.

logic_node.action: Use SGLT2 inhibitors for hyperglycemia management in HF with T2DM
logic_node.action_detail: In patients with HF and type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, sotagliflozin) are recommended as first-line for hyperglycemia management and to reduce HF-related morbidity and mortality. Two RCTs (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced) showed reductions in all-cause death (13%), CV death (14%), HF hospitalization (26%), and renal outcomes (38%).

source_text: In patients with HF and type 2 diabetes, the use of SGLT2i is recommended for the management of hyperglycemia and to reduce HF-related morbidity and mortality. SGLT2i are the first class of glucose-lowering agents to receive approval from the FDA for the treatment of HFrEF.

logic_node.action_detail: Patients on SGLT2 inhibitors should be closely monitored for potential risks including severe genitourinary infections and, less commonly, diabetic ketoacidosis.

source_text: Patients on SGLT2i should be closely monitored for potential risks, including severe genitourinary infections and, less commonly, diabetic ketoacidosis.

logic_node.action: Initiate chronic anticoagulant therapy for AF in HF
logic_node.action_detail: Patients with chronic HF with permanent, persistent, or paroxysmal AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score >=2 (men) or >=3 (women) should receive chronic anticoagulant therapy for stroke prevention.

source_text: Patients with chronic HF with permanent-persistent-paroxysmal AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of >=2 (for men) and >=3 (for women) should receive chronic anticoagulant therapy.

logic_node.action: Prefer DOAC over warfarin for AF in HF
logic_node.action_detail: For patients with chronic HF with permanent, persistent, or paroxysmal AF, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOAC) are recommended over warfarin in eligible patients. DOACs include apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, and dabigatran. DOACs more effectively reduce stroke/systemic embolism, major bleeding, and intracranial bleeding compared with warfarin.

source_text: For patients with chronic HF with permanent-persistent-paroxysmal AF, DOAC is recommended over warfarin in eligible patients. DOACs more effectively reduced the rate of stroke or systemic embolism, major bleeding, and intracranial bleeding compared with warfarin.

logic_node.action: Consider AF ablation for symptom relief in HF
logic_node.action_detail: For patients with HF and symptoms caused by AF, catheter ablation is reasonable to improve symptoms and quality of life. In CASTLE-AF, ablation reduced the composite endpoint of death or rehospitalization (28.5% vs 44.6%). Meta-analysis showed 49% relative risk reduction in mortality and 56% reduction in hospitalizations.

source_text: For patients with HF and symptoms caused by AF, AF ablation is reasonable to improve symptoms and QOL. The composite endpoint of death or rehospitalization was lower in ablation (28.5%) compared with standard care (44.6%).

logic_node.action: Consider AV nodal ablation with CRT implantation
logic_node.action_detail: For patients with AF and LVEF <=50%, if a rhythm control strategy fails or is not desired and ventricular rates remain rapid despite medical therapy, atrioventricular nodal ablation with implantation of a CRT device is reasonable. CRT generally produces more benefit than RV pacing alone.

source_text: For patients with AF and LVEF <=50%, if a rhythm control strategy fails or is not desired, and ventricular rates remain rapid despite medical therapy, atrioventricular nodal ablation with implantation of a CRT device is reasonable.

logic_node.action: Consider anticoagulation even without additional risk factors in HF with AF
logic_node.action_detail: For patients with chronic HF and permanent, persistent, or paroxysmal AF, chronic anticoagulant therapy is reasonable for men and women without additional risk factors (CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1). HF is a hypercoagulable state and independent risk factor for stroke. In patients with HF and CHA2DS2-VASc of 1, those with AF had 3-fold higher risk.

source_text: For patients with chronic HF and permanent-persistent-paroxysmal AF, chronic anticoagulant therapy is reasonable for men and women without additional risk factors. In patients with HF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1, those with AF had a 3-fold higher risk.
